newsitem.title: JAPAN: Any Tokyo aid not for Thai banking sector-sources.
newsitem.headline: Any Tokyo aid not for Thai banking sector-sources.

text.p: Japan may help Thailand shore up its sagging economy and get over the baht crisis, but Bangkok cannot tap Tokyo's coffers to bail out Thai financial institutions, monetary sources said on Wednesday.
Japan's assistance also hinges on whether Bangkok decides to seek help from International Monetary Fund (IMF), they said.

"Any standby credit from the Export-Import Bank of Japan cannot be utilised for the purpose of bad loan write-offs by the banking sector of a particular country," a monetary source told Reuters on Wednesday.
The source said the Ex-Im Bank has not yet made a specific move to open a line of credit to Thailand.
The bank procures funds via bond issues or Japan's Fiscal Investment and Loan Programme, which borrows from deposits of Japanese individual savers and national pension funds.
Another monetary source said there was a chance of Japan providing standby credit to Thailand in the future, but by law it cannot be earmarked for the banking sector.
"Bangkok has only two options -- to print money to provide liquidity for the ailing banking sector, or to borrow from abroad," said Tetsuji Sano, an economist at Nomura Research Institute (NRI).
The latter option appeared more sensible as it was less likely to prompt a spiral of inflation and more baht depreciation, he added.
But Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya reiterated on Wednesday that his government would not borrow from abroad to solve liquidity problems in the financial sector.
He also told reporters the government would announce more measures to bail out the troubled financial sector on July 28.

Analysts said Thailand appears to be hoping to raise some $5 billion in new credit from foreign banks, namely Japanese, and another $5 billion through foreign bond issues, on top of possible standby credit from governments and international aid bodies.
In Tokyo last week, Thanong, while not turning to Japan's government or the IMF for immediate support, asked Japanese banks to maintain credit lines to Thai banks and firms.
Japanese bankers said they were wary of giving new money to Thai banks without other global entities or the Japanese government chipping in for a possible rescue package.
Furthermore, they said their money might well be used for bad loan disposal by Thai banks, despite the fact many Japanese banks themselves are struggling to reduce bad loan holdings.

On Tuesday, Finance One Plc, once Thailand's top finance firm, posted an unaudited loss of 5.23 billion baht for the first half of 1997 versus a profit of 850.31 million baht in the same period last year.

Analysts said Thailand's Financial Institution Development Fund has little financial muscle to deal with the existing bad loan problem. Bangkok is expected to announce the outstanding bad loans held by the financial sector later on Wednesday.
"The real credit crunch in Thailand is still to come as banks have grown even more wary of new lending as the baht float aggravated their balance sheets," said Sano of NRI.
The tumble in the baht's rate to the dollar is putting a heavier repayment burden on banks and firms which originally borrowed dollars and converted them into baht for domestic use.

The baht has lost more than 20 percent of its value since its de facto devaluation on July 2. It was quoted at a new record low of 32.15/50 per dollar in the domestic market on Wednesday, compared with 25.79 per dollar before its flotation.

A foreign bankers' association in Thailand has said it will supply no new credit to local banks and finance companies and that roll-overs of existing loans were available only to the top five banks "at a price" or at higher interest rates.
The ban on roll-overs applied to all finance firms, not just 16 closed by the Bank of Thailand and told to come up with merger or recapitalisation plans.

But not all foreign bankers in Thailand have strictly squeezed credit lines to Thai banks, bankers said. Analysts said that given the heavy exposure to Thailand by Japanese banks and manufacturers, banks were likely to maintain some credit lines despite the move by the foreign bankers' body.
Of Thailand's $89.8 billion in foreign debt, $73 billion is in the form of commercial credits, Thanong said last Thursday.
Japanese bankers estimate their lending to Thai companies represents as much as half of the total commercial credits.
